Energy dense nutritional supplements improve weight gain among malnourished adults with drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis: an open-label randomized controlled trial in Faridabad, India Abstract This open-label randomized controlled trial in India assessed the impact of a peanut-based energy-dense nutritional supplement (EDNS) on weight gain among undernourished adults with drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis in India. EDNS significantly improved weight gain compared to standard care, offering a scalable solution for targeted nutritional support.

Introduction India carries a quarter of the global TB burden.1 Undernutrition, which is associated with 1 increased disease severity and unfavorable outcomes, is the leading driver for TB in India.2 Poor 2 weight gain is associated with increased mortality whereas gaining at least 5% of baseline body 3 weight during the intensive phase is associated with reduced mortality.3,4 4 5 There is a paucity of randomized studies that have reported the impact of macronutrient 6 support on weight gain in persons with tuberculosis (PWTB). Indeed, the 2016 COCHRANE 7 review reported only included five underpowered studies that assessed the impact of 8 macronutrient support on weight gain.2,5 Although PWTB in the RATIONS study showed 9 meaningful weight gain, the lack of a control group makes it difficult to discern the impact of 10 nutritional support. Extrapolating weight gain data from studies of general populations is 11 unwise, as TB induces profound metabolic alterations.2 12 13 Here, we present data from an open-label, randomized-controlled trial of an energy-dense 14 nutritional supplement (EDNS) to understand its impact on weight gain during TB treatment. 15 16 Methods: 17 Study Design and Setting 18 We conducted this open-label, two-arm randomized controlled trial between 2020 and 2023 in 19 two tuberculosis (TB) units in Faridabad district, Haryana, India. Ethics committee of All India 20 Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, approved the study (IEC-110/09.03.2018, RP- 21 23/2018, OP-7/2.8.2019). The trial was registered with Central Trial Registry of India 22 (CTRI/2019/12/022574). 23 24 Participants 25 We enrolled adults (≥18 years) with microbiologically confirmed, drug-sensitive pulmonary TB 26 and mild to moderate undernutrition (BMI 14–18.5 kg/m²) receiving treatment under the 27 National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP). We excluded individuals with peanut allergies, 28 pregnancy or lactation, prior diabetes diagnosis or fasting glucose/HbA1c abnormalities, HIV 29 seropositivity, renal or hepatic impairment, or poor general condition. Participants provided 30 written consent, and the. 31 32 Randomization and Blinding 33 We randomized participants to either the intervention or control arm using a computer- 34 generated sequence and ensured allocation concealment with sequentially numbered, opaque, 35 sealed envelopes. Blinding was not feasible for participants or investigators. 36 37 38 Intervention 39 Participants in the intervention arm received a previously described EDNS weekly alongside 40 standard dietary advice. Each 92 g EDNS sachet provided 500 kcal, 13 g protein, 29 g fat, and 41 micronutrients.6 They consumed two sachets daily for six months or until reaching a BMI of 21 42

kg/m². The control group received only standard dietary advice. Both groups received standard 43 TB treatment. 44 45 Outcome Assessments 46 The primary outcomes were 5% weight gain from baseline at two months and 10% at treatment 47 completion. We weighed participants monthly. Secondary outcomes included EDNS 48 acceptability (assessed via a structured questionnaire on taste, smell, consistency, color, and 49 ease of use after one month), adherence (measured by counting returned empty sachets), 50 adverse effects (recorded biweekly), and hemoglobin improvement. 51 52 Data Collection and Management 53 We collected data electronically using the Open Data Kit (ODK) platform on Android devices and 54 securely stored it on a local MySQL server. 55 56 Statistical Analysis 57 We used box plots to compare percent weight gain in the control and intervention groups over 58 six months. Multivariable logistic regression estimated the adjusted odds ratio for achieving 5% 59 weight gain at month 2 and 10% at treatment completion. A priori, we adjusted for age, sex, 60 asset quintile, and baseline BMI and included covariates with p-values <0.20 in baseline 61 characteristics or univariable regression. We presented acceptability and adverse effect 62 frequencies as proportions. 63 64 Results 65 Recruitment 66 We randomly allocated 335 participants to the intervention or control arm, with 171 in 67 the intervention arm and 164 in the control arm. We subsequently excluded six 68 participants (four intervention, two control) upon detecting multidrug resistance 69 (Supplementary Figure 1). 70 71 Demographics 72 Mean age of participants was not significantly different in the intervention and control arms 73 (33.1 ± 13.4 vs. 33.4 ± 14.7 years, p = 0.802). There was a higher proportion of men in the 74 control arm (65.9% vs. 59.2%). The mean BMI of participants (p= 0.25) and distribution across 75 wealth quintiles (p= 0.701) were similar between arms. (Supplementary table 1) 76 77 Weight gain trends: 78 Participants in the intervention group gained a higher percentage of their baseline body weight 79 in both the intensive phase and the continuation phase. (Figure 1).At the end of the intensive 80 phase, a high proportion of PWTB in the intervention arm had gained 5% of their body weight 81 (53.9% vs. 39.3%, p= 0.015). Similarly, at the end of treatment, a higher proportion of 82 intervention arm participants gained 10% of their baseline body weight (55.8% vs. 41.0%, 83 p=0.023). (Supplementary table 2). 84 85 Primary outcomes 86

After adjusting for age, sex, baseline BMI, asset quintile, and alcohol use, intervention group 87 participants had higher odds of 5% body weight gain at month 2 (adjust odds ratio [aOR]: 2.02 88 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.25-3.30). Intervention group participants also had higher odds 89 of gaining 10% body weight by month 6 (aOR: 1.89 (95% CI: 1.13-3.18). (Supplementary table 3) 90 91 Secondary outcomes 92 Acceptability and adherence 93 All participants (100%) found the sachet easy to open, though only 76.2% fully understood the 94 instructions. Taste was acceptable to 96.7%, smell to 99.1%, and consistency to 99.9% of 95 participants. Study personnel observed positive facial expressions in 76.2% of instances. 96 Additionally, 89.9% of participants reported subjective health improvements after consuming 97 EDNS. Adherence was high, with an overall rate of 88.7%, with 71% of participants never 98 missing a sachet. 99 100 Adverse Events 101 Nausea and vomiting were more frequent in the intervention group, occurring in 10.2% vs. 4.3% 102 (p = 0.055) and 7.5% vs. 3.6% (p = 0.149) of observed weeks, respectively. Abdominal fullness 103 was also higher (12.9% vs. 5.4%, p = 0.032). Other adverse effects did not significantly differ 104 between groups. (Supplementary table 4) 105 106 Hemoglobin recovery 107 Mean hemoglobin at baseline was 10.8 g/dL (SD 2.0). The hemoglobin gain at 2 months was 0.7 108 g/dL (SD 1.8) in the EDNS arm and 0.5 g/dL (SD 1.6) in the control arm (p=0.315), while at 6 109 months, it was 1.0 g/dL (SD 2.0) in the EDNS arm and 1.1 g/dL (SD 1.7) in the control arm 110 (p=0.830). 111 112 Discussion: 113 To our knowledge, this is the largest randomized controlled trial to assess the impact of 114 macronutrient support using a ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) on weight gain among 115 PWTB. We found that undernourished PWTB receiving EDNS gained more weight. Importantly, a 116 higher proportion of EDNS recipients gained 5% body weight by the end of the intensive phase. 117 This study provides a strong rationale for the use of EDNS to enhance the nutritional recovery of 118 PWTB. 119 120 Notably, the weight gain among EDNS recipients was comparable to that seen among PWTB in 121 the RATIONS study, which provided food baskets with 1200 Kcal per day. The RATIONS study 122 PWTB had a mean baseline BMI of 16.4 (SD: 2.5) which was comparable to that of our 123 participants. At month 2, 53.9% of EDNS recipients gained 5% of their baseline body weight, 124 which was similar to the 54% of PWTB in RATIONS who attained the same metric. At the end of 125 month 6, EDNS recipients had a median 11.7% weight gain (IQR: 6.1-18.1) which is almost 126 identical to the RATIONS study (median 11.6%, IQR: 6.4-17.4). This comparison provides 127 confidence that RUTFs such as EDNS are comparable to food baskets in improving weight gain. 128 129

One significant drawback of food baskets is the uncertainty about PWTB getting an adequate 130 caloric load. Parents may instead prioritize their children’s nutrition, for instance. Gender 131 dynamics may also come into play. Further, time-consuming preparation and fuel poverty may 132 also inhibit the utilization of food baskets. And while Indian PWTB receive cash transfers 133 through the Nikshay Poshan Yojana, the impact of cash transfers on tangible nutritional metrics 134 among PWTB remains uncertain. RUTFs such as EDNS have been vetted in numerous clinical 135 studies for use in contexts such as severe-acute malnutrition.7 Providing a dedicated nutritional 136 supplement to persons with TB may help them attain a suitable caloric load, improving drug 137 absorption, and potentially reducing drug toxicity, relapse, and mortality, particularly if provided 138 promptly at treatment initiation.8 Moreover, the EDNS can be modified to meet the needs of 139 special populations such as those with diabetes. 140 141 This study has several limitations. First, as an open-label trial, the lack of participant and 142 investigator blinding may have introduced biases. Second, the study was conducted in two TB 143 units in Faridabad which may limit generalizability to regions with different socio-economic or 144 cultural contexts. Third, unmeasured factors such as dietary variations outside the intervention 145 or social determinants of health could have influenced the outcomes. Finally, the exclusion of 146 certain high-risk populations, such as those with diabetes or HIV, limits the applicability of our 147 findings to these key and vulnerable subgroups. More research is needed to optimize the 148 composition of EDNS for these populations as well as for children and pregnant women. 149 150 Our study demonstrates that EDNS effectively enhances weight gain among undernourished 151 PWTB while being acceptable and with minimal adverse events, offering a practical and scalable 152 solution for targeted caloric and micronutrient delivery. However, EDNS alone cannot resolve 153 the widespread food insecurity faced by many PWTB. An integrated approach, as proposed by 154 India’s National TB Elimination Program— combining cash transfers, food baskets, and EDNS-- 155 may provide a more comprehensive and sustainable strategy to improve nutritional outcomes 156 and treatment success than any of these strategies. 157
